entry_claim_bounded: Behistun repeats the king's accession/victory claim across Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian scribal traditions as monumental royal display with different composition histories and coverage; Old Persian's attested corpus is dominated by royal inscriptions and is not thereby the language of every imperial subject; monumental trilingualism does not exclude other widely used administrative media, with the Persepolis Fortification records documenting daily provisioning chiefly in Elamite (plus an Aramaic strand, and an Old Persian and a Greek tablet); the Stolper-Tavernier Old Persian administrative tablet (Fort. 1208-101) is a real counterexample to 'Old Persian = display only' that does not by itself demonstrate general practical use; and archive language does not directly count spoken-language populations.

corroborations.label: corroboration_2_cdlb_elamite_edition
corroborations.source_citation: Saber Amiri Parian (2017), 'A New Edition of the Elamite Version of the Behistun Inscription (I)', Cuneiform Digital Library Bulletin 2017:3 (ISSN 1540-8760), published 2017-12-22, CC BY 4.0.
corroborations.source_locator: §2.1 ('The inscription') and §3.1 ('The text of the Elamite version'); section headings as returned live
corroborations.source_excerpt: This monument consists of a relief sculpture and a tri-lingual inscription in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian Akkadian. ... The older Elamite version of the Behistun inscription was engraved to the right of the sculptured reliefs. But since it became necessary later to make room for the relief of the captured Scythian rebel "Skunxa," this version was erased by the same engravers and then, as its copy, the newer Elamite version was written beneath the Babylonian version.
corroborations.retrieval_method: Live fetch this round. https://cdli.ucla.edu/pubs/cdlb/2017/cdlb2017_003.html failed with curl error 6 'Could not resolve host: cdli.ucla.edu' (2026-10-17T20:17Z); the article was retrieved from the CDLI mirror cdli.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de (HTTP 200, 146,529 bytes) and cross-checked against cdli.earth (HTTP 200, identical 146,529 bytes); tag-stripped text located by string search. corroborations.relevance: Independent peer-reviewed statement that Behistun is a trilingual monument and that the versions have different composition histories (the first Elamite version erased and re-engraved beneath the Babylonian version, 54 paragraphs in the newer Elamite version). Supports the entry's line 54 'different composition histories and coverage' without endorsing any translation-mistake reading. This article does not itself discuss the column-five appendix.

basis: All four checkable legs of the residual now carry fresh round-8 passages. (1) The main source was re-fetched this round by a new route (Wayback capture id_ 20250922051004) because the live URL timed out; its sha256 equals the parent's round-6 copy, and the 'practical' text quotation sits on PDF/printed page 9, confirming the parent's corrected locator. The passage keeps the counterexample bounded: 'It may not demonstrate general use of Old Persian.' (2) The round-6 blocker on Hallock's pages is cleared: OIP 92's own PDF is now reachable and its printed pp. 6 and 42-43 were read first-hand, supplying the entry's glossary wording (halmi 'sealed document', miyatukkam 'authorization', pirradaziš persons 'fast messenger' / horses 'express', title status uncertain) and the archive's regional confinement to Persis and southern Elam. (3) Behistun's cross-version gap is re-verified from the entry's cited overview page: the Babylonian and Elamite panels lack the column-five appendix, while a peer-reviewed Elamite edition independently documents the versions' different composition histories. (4) The monumental-versus-administrative distinction is reinforced by ARTA p. 2 ('three strands of a single information system') and p. 22 ('interplay among several streams of information', with Greek and Old Persian tablets as latitude, and Lewis's remark that 'At the level of speech … the position will have been even worse'). The compound claim is nevertheless not upgraded to whole-claim support: no retrieved passage speaks to the languages actually spoken by imperial subjects, and the appendix-absence statement rests on a reference page rather than an edition.
coupling_implication: The entry's layered model (dynastic voice, authorized translation, provincial legal usage, oral proclamation, archival record) now has fresh textual anchors at both ends: the monumental trilingual display with its version asymmetries, and the everyday Elamite/Aramaic provisioning machinery with credentials that survive only by citation. For a worldbuilding system this means the royal voice, the credential, and the receipt can be modeled as three distinct artifacts even inside one institution — exactly the entry's design transfer at line 57 and its credential-versus-record row at line 119.
limits: The ARTA retrieval is a fresh fetch of the same artifact (identical sha256 to the round-6 copy), not a new edition; its 'practical text' sentence remains an isolate statement by its authors. The Hallock evidence is OCR of a 1969 printed scan: diacritics and formatting are partly lost, page numbers were mapped from running heads (PDF 14='4', 18='8', 20='10', 22='12', 24='14', 52='42', 53='43'), and the quotes are transcribed as OCR'd. The Behistun appendix statement comes from an educational reference page (the entry's own access aid), not from an edition or collation; the physical state of the Elamite and Babylonian panels (damage versus absence) was not inspected, and the Iranica version article could not be retrieved (403) so no scholarly cross-check of that specific sentence exists in this receipt. No source retrieved this round establishes the spoken languages of subject populations, and none is claimed; archive languages are treated strictly as institutional media. No PDF or extraction is published in the repository; artifacts live only in the git-ignored scratch reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round8-f11/.
transcription_notes: Hallock OIP 92 is OCR of a printed scan: line-break hyphenation was joined when quoting ('authoriz-ing documents' -> 'authorizing documents'), and one run-together token is reproduced as scanned ('(pirradaziS)horses').
The Livius page's link markup introduces a space before a closing parenthesis inside the quoted sentence ('Achaemenid Empire )'); it was normalized to 'Empire)' when quoting.

Every quoted passage in this receipt was machine-checked against the retrieved artifacts (whitespace normalization, HTML tag removal, hyphenation joining): the main excerpt, the leg excerpts and all corroboration excerpts match their sources modulo the two normalizations documented in the two notes above.
